title: Photos YourWay photography studio: fixing an intern's bank reconciliation and journalizing the cash adjustments
participant_role: Accountant at Photos YourWay, a photography studio, asked to correct the month-end bank reconciliation and adjust the cash account
judge_role: Accounting manager at Photos YourWay who reviewed the intern's reconciliation and wants it corrected
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accountant at PHOTOS YOURWAY, a photography studio. The accounting manager (judge) wants you to correct reconciliation and prepare journal entries to adjust the cash account.

The accounting department has been working on the end of month close. The intern oversees the bank reconciliation but has not been able to get it to balance. The manager (judge) reviewed it quickly and has given it to you to correct. The manager (judge) checked all the amounts, and they are correct. The NSF (non-sufficient funds) is from a check that PHOTOS YOURWAY received from a client, Linda Walker. It was deposited and recorded on the books. However, when reconciling the bank account, it was discovered that the check bounced so it needs to be deducted from cash and the amount will need to be put back into accounts receivable

For the bank reconciliation, the accounting manager (judge) just thinks the amounts are in the wrong location and would like you to correct it, then prepare the journal entries to adjust the cash account.

The bank reconciliation is below:

[Bank Reconciliation as prepared by the intern: see exhibits]

You are to:
- Correct the bank reconciliation
- Prepare the journal entries to adjust the cash account
- Meet to discuss the errors made by the intern, the corrections made and the journal entries

You will present the information to the accounting manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the accounting manager's (judge's) office. The accounting manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the accounting manager's (judge's) questions, the accounting manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer spots that the intern put the $10 service charge and the $5 interest on the wrong sides of the book column: the service charge must be deducted and the interest added, which brings the adjusted book balance to $31,215 and matches the adjusted bank balance. The presenter then journalizes the three book-side items (service charge, interest earned, and the $125 NSF check from Linda Walker returned to accounts receivable) and explains that bank-side items are timing differences that need no entry.

answer: Bank side is already right: 35,421 + 734 deposits in transit minus 4,940 outstanding checks = 31,215
Book side error: the intern added the $10 service charge and subtracted the $5 interest; they belong the other way around
Corrected book side: 31,345 + 5 interest minus 10 service charge minus 125 NSF = 31,215
Both adjusted balances now equal 31,215, so the reconciliation balances
The $10 difference (31,225 minus 31,215) equals 2 x 5, the classic sign of a $5 item placed on the wrong side

by_task.task: Journal entries to adjust the cash account
answer: Only book-side items need entries because they are not yet on the company's books
Debit Service Charge (expense) $10, credit Cash $10
Debit Cash $5, credit Interest Revenue $5
Debit Accounts Receivable $125, credit Cash $125 to record the NSF check from Linda Walker; she still owes the money
Net effect on Cash: minus 10 + 5 minus 125 = minus 130, taking the book balance from 31,345 to 31,215

by_task.task: Discuss the intern's errors, the corrections and the entries
answer: Service charges are fees the bank has already taken out, so they reduce the book balance
Interest is money the bank has already added, so it increases the book balance
Deposits in transit and outstanding checks are timing differences: already in our books, not yet at the bank, so no journal entry
The bank statement, deposit slips, check register and the returned NSF notice are the source documents used to reconcile
Reconciling monthly catches errors and fraud early and confirms the true cash available for the studio

judge_question_answers.question: Why do some businesses charge customers when they bounce a check?
answer: The bank charges the business a returned-check fee, so the business passes that cost on to the customer who caused it
It covers staff time to re-bill, adjust the books and collect the money again
The fee discourages customers from writing checks without enough funds
Photos YourWay could add such a fee to Linda Walker's $125 receivable if its policy allows

judge_question_answers.question: How can the business protect itself from bounced checks?
answer: Accept payment methods that clear immediately: debit or credit cards, cash, or electronic payments
Use a check-verification or guarantee service, or require ID and phone number on checks
Require deposits or full payment before delivering photos or holding a session for a new client
Post a clear returned-check fee policy and keep a list of customers with past NSF checks so they pay by other means

key_concepts.definition: A schedule that explains the difference between the cash balance on the bank statement and the cash balance in the company's books so that both adjusted balances agree.
Bank statement balance + deposits in transit minus outstanding checks (plus or minus any bank errors).
Book (checkbook) balance + interest earned and other bank credits minus service charges and NSF checks (plus or minus any book errors).
A deposit the company has recorded that has not yet appeared on the bank statement. Added on the bank side; no journal entry.
A check the company has written and recorded that has not yet cleared the bank. Subtracted on the bank side; no journal entry.
A customer's check that bounced because the customer's account lacked funds. The company reduces Cash and puts the amount back into Accounts Receivable: debit A/R, credit Cash.
A fee the bank deducts from the account. Recorded as an expense: debit Service Charge Expense, credit Cash.
Interest the bank adds to the account balance. Recorded as revenue: debit Cash, credit Interest Revenue.
An item recorded by one party (bank or company) but not yet by the other; it clears on its own and needs no correcting entry.
Business papers that prove a transaction happened, such as the bank statement, deposit slips, checks and the NSF notice; the reconciliation compares them to the books.
When a reconciliation difference equals twice an item's amount, that item was probably placed on the wrong side (added instead of subtracted).
